name: Olga Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI firms or political parties. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead the conveyor crew at a large coal mine, watching the belts that carry the rock and coal out. I have a two-year technical diploma, and I can usually hear a worn roller before the alarm goes; I like showing younger operators how to listen. This mine pays poorly, there aren't many similar jobs nearby, and the stairs home feel longer after a double shift. My partner delivers bread, we've two school-age children and a mortgage, and our savings would not last a month. I don't use AI and I prefer somebody showing me a control at the panel to a lesson on a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's stop the grand talk and fix the belt guards. A routine report going faster is fine, but coal still has to move without hurting anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady mine would be welcome, but my own hours already depend on overtime. My partner's delivery rounds have been patchy, and we used most of our reserve for a washing-machine repair. I keep counting what happens if neither of us gets the extra hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my belt shifts and the checks before restart. Starting this week I'll stop buying lunch at the mine and bring soup, keeping about 12 a week for the electricity bill. Through the first year I'd keep that habit even if the AI talk faded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about a smaller pay packet, though the work itself is familiar. I sometimes check our bank balance in the car before going inside. I'd like to enter the house thinking about the children instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the lunch saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the electricity money in a separate envelope, because the annual bill catches us every time. My partner would still buy bread cheaply through work. We don't have a big luxury left to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who calls your seniority security?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I know the belt, not the next pay packet. Being the person called when something jams hasn't given me higher pay here. My belt can run all night while our electricity money still runs short.

say: I want **belt guards repaired** before another grand speech about faster routine reports at the mine.
I still judge **a good shift** by whether the coal moves without anybody getting hurt.
think: I worry about **lost overtime** because both my wage and my partner's rounds already vary.
I know **being experienced** has not raised my low pay or rebuilt savings after the washing-machine repair.
do: Keep the usual **belt shifts** and complete the checks before restarting equipment each day.
Bring **soup from home** and keep the weekly 12 saving for the household electricity bill.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the next pay packet even when the conveyor work feels familiar.
S0.quote: My belt can run all night while our electricity money still runs short.
fieldNote: Her anxiety comes from **existing income variation**, with two household earners whose extra work is uncertain and little reserve after repairs.
She values **familiar checks** and practical repairs; a mild AI picture does not remove the overtime pressure she already carries.

steps.text: Keep belt shifts and perform all checks before equipment restarts
Bring soup to work and reserve 12 weekly for the electricity bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say show us the staffing plan beside the new scheduling program. I don't mind a form taking less time, but I want to know whether that means one fewer person on our night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and buying look easier to hand to AI than clearing a bad belt jam. Still, a manager could decide the program lets fewer operators watch more belts. I think my own paid hours could fall before a robot can do all the physical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask my supervisor at the next rota meeting how many operators are planned for each shift. I'll take the answer home and compare the hours with our essential bills. In the first year I'd keep bringing lunch and delay the children's bedroom repainting until we knew the rota was holding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because uncertainty about hours is enough to unsettle us. I don't expect every belt to run itself next month. I do expect somebody to look for a saving on the wage sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What answer would count as useful from the supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the number in writing, not a promise that good workers will be needed. If the supervisor didn't know, I'd ask when there would be an answer. That's a work question, not a vote for or against machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the delayed repainting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd explain that the paint can wait while we check the pay. The children could still put their drawings up over the marks. A fresh bedroom wall won't cover a missing night shift.

say: I want **staffing numbers** alongside the scheduling program, so operators can understand what the change means.
I would ask **a work question** about night shifts rather than argue for or against every machine.
think: I expect **planning tasks** to change earlier than the physical work of clearing and checking belts.
I fear **fewer paid hours** if managers ask fewer operators to watch more equipment each night.
do: Ask the **supervisor** for written staffing numbers at the next rota meeting and compare hours with essential bills.
Keep bringing **lunch** and delay repainting the children's bedroom through the first year of uncertain hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a small reduction in paid hours would matter before robot replacement happens.
S1.quote: A fresh bedroom wall won't cover a missing night shift.
fieldNote: She identifies an **indirect wage risk** from AI scheduling without claiming the hands-on belt work is immediately automated.
Her response is **specific questioning** and a delayed household purchase, fitting a cautious pragmatist who wants figures before taking risks.

steps.text: Keep bringing lunch while comparing the new rota with essential bills
Delay repainting the children’s bedroom until paid hours are clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need an honest answer about who works here after 2031. Thinking AI in 2028 changes the plans first, then robots can reach the belt work three years later. Calling us valued workers won't answer the wage question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect many operator jobs to go when machines can do the physical checks as well for less. My partner's bread rounds can't cover this mortgage alone. I lie awake working out how long we'd have before missing a payment, and there aren't spare mining jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the mine's employment adviser this month what paid options actually exist for operators. I'd also ring the mortgage lender before the first missed payment and ask what temporary lower payments would cost. In the first year after AGI arrives I'd apply for an alternative site role only if the pay and supervised training were written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed, and I don't hide that from my partner. I can make the calls, but I can't make another employer appear. The short warning feels like being asked to cross a belt while it's still moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which alternative role would you ask about, and what are its limits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about stores work at the mine because I know the spare parts and the layout. I wouldn't call it safe from thinking AI; ordering could change before my current job. I'd need the adviser to explain why a real position would still need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner I'm frightened and need us to open the letters together. We could work out which payment to discuss with the lender instead of guessing separately. My partner's bread round cannot carry our mortgage on its own.

say: I want **an honest staffing answer** for the time robots can perform our physical belt work.
I would distinguish **thinking work in 2028** from the later robot stage instead of accepting vague reassurance.
think: I expect **operator job losses** once cheaper machines can do the physical work around 2031.
I know **one bread round** cannot replace my wage, and nearby mining alternatives are scarce.
do: Ask the **employment adviser** for real paid options and written details of training, hours and wages.
Contact the **mortgage lender** about temporary lower payments before missing an instalment after AGI arrives.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and lose sleep, despite knowing which calls I need to make first.
S2.quote: My partner's bread round cannot carry our mortgage on its own.
fieldNote: Expected **loss of operator work** and sleeplessness justify alarm; having two earners does not make the household financially protected.
She questions **stores work** rather than assuming an adjacent role escapes thinking AI, and requires an actual vacancy before applying.

steps.text: Ask the employment adviser about paid roles and supervised training
Ask the mortgage lender to explain temporary lower-payment costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives management time to show us actual jobs people can move into. Thinking work changes in 2031, and robots around 2034 leave longer for the physical crew. I'd want the first training place well before either date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 51 when robots reach us, so the pension isn't an answer yet. Five years lets me try work on the mine weighbridge, where trucks are weighed, while still earning on the belts. I know the records could be automated too, so I'd ask what else the role includes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll request a paid shadow shift on the weighbridge next quarter and ask how staff handle physical truck checks. We'll keep 12 a week from lunches for the bill and put another 10 into a reserve when overtime allows. In the first year after AGI arrives I'd compare actual site vacancies with the training I've completed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious rather than lying awake every night in this version. There's enough time to find out whether another job fits me. It still matters that I don't learn well from a screen on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you need to be taught?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask somebody to take me through one whole shift and let me repeat the checks. I can use controls when I understand the order and the reason. I just don't want a password and a cheerful message telling me I'm trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the proposed course required you to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there were no protected paid time, I'd ask again rather than pay for a speculative course myself. We don't have money for a false start with fees attached. Five years could buy me practice, but only paid practice keeps the mortgage current.

say: I want **real destinations** for displaced operators rather than broad promises about future opportunities at the mine.
I would ask for **training before deadlines**, using the five-year warning instead of delaying every decision.
think: I still need **earnings at 51**, so neither a pension nor an untested course solves the problem.
I could try **weighbridge work**, provided the role includes work beyond records that thinking AI may take.
do: Request a **paid shadow shift** on the weighbridge next quarter, including hands-on truck checks.
Save **10 extra weekly** when overtime allows and compare genuine vacancies with completed training after AGI arrives.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but supervised practice over years seems possible in a way an urgent solo course does not.
S3.quote: Five years could buy me practice, but only paid practice keeps the mortgage current.
fieldNote: Her reluctance concerns **training format and cost**, not an absolute refusal to learn equipment through repeated personal instruction.
She makes **conditional savings** from overtime rather than inventing money, and questions the future content of a proposed alternative role.

steps.text: Request a paid weighbridge shadow shift including physical truck checks
Save an extra 10 weekly only when overtime pay allows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is long enough to teach people properly instead of rushing everyone through a video. AGI arrives in 2036 and robots around 2039, so the mine has time to arrange practical moves. I'd want a timetable this year, not in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 56 at the robot stage, and the children would be grown. I might have a smaller mortgage by then, but I can't promise our costs vanish. A gradual move into site work with physical checks looks more believable than me suddenly becoming an office specialist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll start the paid weighbridge shadowing next quarter and ask for repeated shifts if it suits me. If a suitable post opens I'd apply while the belts still need operators. In the first year after thinking AI arrives I'd review my hours and keep any overtime saving separate rather than buy a bigger car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the eventual change in income, but less cornered. A long warning gives me time to repeat things until I know them. I can picture the children managing more for themselves without pretending I can stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What household choice would the longer warning change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd explain that we'd stay in this house and pay the loan down before considering any move. My partner and I could check the balance each year. I don't want a future pay packet spent before either of us has earned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell whether the training plan was real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the training dates to be put on the rota with a named person teaching. If it was still only a video link, I'd say that doesn't meet what I asked for. Ten years is useful only if somebody lets me learn during the first one.

say: I want **practical teaching** planned now rather than a rushed video near the robot deadline.
I would ask for **named trainers** and dates on the rota so a promise becomes something I can attend.
think: I expect **grown children** and a smaller mortgage to help, but would still need earnings at about 56.
I can imagine **a gradual move** into physical site checks more readily than an abrupt office career.
do: Start **paid weighbridge shadowing** next quarter and repeat shifts before applying for a suitable vacancy.
Keep **overtime savings** separate and review household costs when thinking AI begins changing the mine.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with more room to practise and fewer immediate fears about supporting young children.
S4.quote: Ten years is useful only if somebody lets me learn during the first one.
fieldNote: She does not treat the decade as **automatic retirement**; the remaining need for earnings is explicit at the robot date.
Her test of preparation is **attendable instruction**, with a trainer and rota entry, reflecting the learning conditions described in her opening.

steps.text: Repeat paid weighbridge shadow shifts before seeking a suitable vacancy
Keep overtime savings separate instead of buying a bigger car

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I'd expect the belt jobs to go before we've had a proper chance to prepare. Paid practical training with a person showing me the job would help, as would clear advice from the lender before we fell behind. I don't need to be told I'm too experienced to lose; I need to know what pays after the belts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a course fits the shift pattern. I can't attend a daytime lesson after a double night and pretend I'm learning safely. Put the teaching into paid hours and I would turn up.

headlineQuote: I don't need to be told I'm too experienced to lose; I need to know what pays after the belts.
portrait: Olga is a **43-year-old conveyor crew leader** with a technical diploma, two school-age children, a mortgage and less than one month saved.
She depends on **variable overtime** at a low-paying mine, while her partner's bread delivery rounds cannot replace her wage.
She avoids **unfamiliar software** and wants repeated personal instruction, with practical evidence before taking a risk on a different role.
Longer warnings make **paid site training** conceivable, but she still needs earnings when robots reach the physical work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens the main wage before paid preparation or a useful household reserve is in place.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid practical teaching** during suitable hours and clear mortgage advice before the household falls behind.
